L16: vessels of the Classical Harappan pottery, the black slipped jar stands out due to its peculiar shape and relative scarcity. This tall, pear-shaped jar has a rather constricted throat, large bulbous body and an elongated narrow base (fig.2 & 3). The base is so narrow that the vessel cannot stand on it without external support. Although it is regarded as a household storage vessel (Marshall 1931), its actual use has always been shrouded in mystery.
L17: One always wondered how and what did the Harappans store in this unsteady vessel? T Gujarat, during the first field-season in 1996 brought to light a large number of black slipped jar sherds including a large rim bearing a graffiti in Harappan script on it (fig.1). Over 200 sherds of this pottery along with many other Classical Harappan remains were unearthed from the site in the subsequent years. This is one of the largest collections of black slipped jar sherds reported from Gujarat Harappan sites.
L18: Among the several well-known characteristic The Black Slipped Jar (BSJ) is widely regarded as a vessel used by the Harappans for overseas transportation of goods. The discovery of considerable number of BSJs from Bagasra, a site located in the Saurashtra coast of the Gulf of Kachchh, indicates the presence of Harappan traders at the site as early as the middle of third millennium BCE.
L19: Fluctuating volume of Harappan trade through time is reflected in the relative abundance of the vessel unearthed in different phases of Harappan occupation at the site. Close correspondence of metrical features of the BSJs from Bagasra with the Indus valley sites suggests certain degree of standardization in their production. Graffiti in Harappan script on BSJ appear to be linked with operational aspects of the trade involving the vessel.

L138: The black slipped jar is a rare vessel even
L139: 
L140: in Harappan sites in the Indus valley. It is
L141: 
L142: reported only from a few important sites
L143: 
L144: such as Mohenjodaro, Harappa, Nausharo
L145: 
L146: and Chanhudaro in Pakistan (Fig.4). Its
L147: distribution in the Gagghar-Saraswati basin
L148: 
L149: in Haryana and Rajasthan, and further
L150: 
L151: south in Gujarat is also limited to a very few
L152: 
L153: sites. However, the discovery of several black
L154: 
L155: slipped jar sherds along with other Harappan
L156: 
L157: relics from a number of Chalcolithic sites in
L158: 
L159: the Oman peninsula (Cleuziou 1984, 1992,
L160: 
L161: Edens 1993, Tosi 1993, Méry 1996) added
L162: 
L163: a new dimension to the significance of
L164: 
L165: the vessel. Clay matching analysis of the
L166: 
L167: Oman vessels clearly indicated their Indus
L168: valley origin (Méry and Blackman n.d.). It
L169: 
L170: has therefore been suggested that the black
L171: 
L172: slipped jar was a container specially used
L173: 
L174: for overseas transportation of goods by the
L175: 
L176: Harappans. Its peculiar shape with the long,
L177: 
L178: narrow bottom belies this argument. In other
L179: 
L180: words, the black slipped jar was a vessel
L181: 
L182: associated with long distance Harappan
L183: 
L184: trade and therefore its presence at any given
L185: 
L186: site indicated the Harappan trade contact.
L187: 
L188: An interesting corollary of this argument is
L189: that coastal Harappan sites hold a better
L190: 
L191: potential for the presence of black slipped
L192: 
L193: jars than landlocked sites. Therefore, the
L194: 
L195: geographical distribution of this vessel in
L196: 
L197: the vast Harappan domain is particularly
L198: 
L199: significant in understanding the dynamism
L200: 
L201: of the Harappan trade. This paper discusses
L202: 
L203: the stratigraphic and cultural context of
L204: 
L205: the black slipped jar from the coastal site
L206: 
L207: at Bagasra in Jamnagar district and the
L208: 
L209: significance of its distribution in Gujarat in
L210: the background of Harappan trade.
